patient.chief_complaint: Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and sudden bilateral hearing loss with dizziness over 3 days
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Nguyen Van Minh is a 56-year-old right-handed Vietnamese pig farmer who presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, progressively worsening headache, neck stiffness, and bilateral hearing loss with dizziness. Three days ago he developed an abrupt onset of high fever (measured at 39.4 degrees Celsius at home), severe throbbing headache, chills, and nausea with one episode of vomiting. He initially attributed the illness to fatigue from farm work. The following morning he noticed he was unable to hear his wife calling him from the next room and described the sound in both ears as markedly muffled, as though his ears were stuffed with cotton. He also developed a feeling of swirling dizziness and became unsteady on his feet, needing to hold onto walls to walk. His wife took him to a local district clinic where the physician found the ear canals and tympanic membranes normal on otoscopy and attributed his hearing loss and dizziness to bilateral acute labyrinthitis or inner-ear viral infection. He was prescribed oral betahistine and sent home with instructions to rest. Despite this treatment, over the subsequent 24 hours his headache intensified substantially, his neck became increasingly stiff, and he developed photophobia. He also became progressively drowsy. His wife brought him to the regional hospital emergency department this morning. She reports he slept most of the journey and was difficult to rouse. He denies any prior ear infection, ear trauma, or noise exposure. He has no history of meningitis or encephalitis. Regarding occupational exposures: he routinely handles raw pork and pig carcasses without gloves when slaughtering animals on his farm; he slaughtered two pigs and prepared raw pork approximately 4 days before symptom onset. He does not recall any skin lacerations at the time but cannot be certain. He has not received meningococcal, pneumococcal, or any other relevant vaccination. His diabetes is reasonably controlled on oral medication. There is no known sick contact with meningitis.

results.title: Streptococcus suis Meningitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
results.summary: Systematic review of 1,584 human S. suis cases globally. Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is the dominant complication, occurring in approximately 50-66% of cases. Vestibular dysfunction co-occurs in approximately 20-30% of patients. Risk factors: occupational swine contact, raw pork handling, skin abrasions during slaughter. Third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone) are the treatment of choice; penicillin G is an alternative for susceptible isolates. Blood cultures are frequently negative in S. suis meningitis despite positive CSF culture. Evidence level: systematic review.

results.title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis (IDSA 2004)
results.summary: Empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults: third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h) plus vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h). Adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h for 4 days should be administered before or with the first antibiotic dose; reduces mortality and hearing loss in bacterial meningitis adults. Evidence level: guideline.

results.title: Dexamethasone in adults with bacterial meningitis
results.summary: Randomized controlled trial demonstrating adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h for 4 days) begun before or with first antibiotics significantly reduces unfavourable outcomes and death in bacterial meningitis. Hearing-loss reduction also observed. Benefit most pronounced in pneumococcal disease but trial included streptococcal species. Evidence level: RCT.

output.summary: Streptococcus suis causes occupational zoonotic bacterial meningitis predominantly in pig farmers and raw-pork handlers in Southeast and East Asia. Sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction are hallmark complications and may be the presenting features, predating full meningismus. Standard multiplex PCR meningitis panels do not include S. suis; MALDI-TOF or sequencing is required for definitive identification. Empiric regimen: ceftriaxone plus vancomycin; de-escalate to ceftriaxone or penicillin G monotherapy for susceptible isolates. Adjunctive dexamethasone given before or with first antibiotic dose is recommended and may reduce severity of cochlear inflammation.

optimal_actions.action: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose and send CBC with differential, CMP, procalcitonin, CRP, and lactate.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Peripheral leukocytosis with marked neutrophilia and left shift; markedly elevated CRP and procalcitonin consistent with bacterial sepsis. Note: blood cultures may be negative in S. suis meningitis as bacteremia is frequently transient.

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture with opening-pressure measurement and send CSF for cell count with differential, glucose (with concurrent serum glucose), protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, and CSF lactate.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Markedly elevated opening pressure, marked PMN-predominant pleocytosis, very low CSF:serum glucose ratio, markedly elevated protein, Gram-positive cocci on Gram stain; culture grows alpha-hemolytic Gram-positive cocci subsequently identified as S. suis by MALDI-TOF.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ceftriaxone as first-line for susceptible S. suis; IDSA empiric regimen (ceftriaxone + vancomycin); De Gans 2002 RCT supporting dexamethasone for hearing-loss reduction in bacterial meningitis.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Dexamethasone antagonizes glycemic control in diabetic patient on metformin — glucose monitoring and insulin coverage required; no absolute contraindications; ceftriaxone is first-line for penicillin-susceptible isolate.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of infective endocarditis (no heart murmur, no embolic phenomena, negative blood cultures, no sustained bacteremia); echocardiography is not part of the routine S. suis meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to the diagnosis or management of bacterial meningitis.
ECG has no role in the diagnosis or management of bacterial meningitis in this otherwise cardiac-healthy patient.
PET imaging has no role in acute pyogenic meningitis; CT and MRI cover all indicated imaging indications.

sequence_constraints.reason: Blood cultures must be drawn before the first antibiotic dose to preserve microbiological yield. This patient has GCS 13 without focal deficits, papilledema, or severe immunocompromise and is under age 60; CT before LP is not mandated, but peripheral cultures must precede antibiotics.

critical_actions: Draw two sets of blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose to preserve microbiological yield.
Perform lumbar puncture — CT before LP is not mandated in this immunocompetent patient under 60 without focal deficits, papilledema, or severely depressed consciousness (GCS 13).
Administer empiric IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h + vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do not delay for culture speciation.
Administer adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose to reduce mortality and limit the severity of cochlear inflammation; continue q6h for 4 days.
Elicit and document occupational swine-contact and raw-pork handling history — this exposure history is essential for identifying S. suis as the likely organism and is the key epidemiological clue.

Recognise that bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction is the hallmark early complication of S. suis meningitis and must not be misattributed to primary labyrinthitis when fever and headache are present.
Note that standard multiplex PCR meningitis panels (e.g., FilmArray ME) do not include S. suis; definitive identification requires culture and MALDI-TOF or sequencing.
De-escalate antibiotics after susceptibility results: confirmed penicillin-susceptible S. suis may be treated with penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h or ceftriaxone monotherapy.
Arrange audiology follow-up after recovery — S. suis sensorineural hearing loss is frequently permanent and requires hearing-aid or cochlear-implant evaluation.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT attribute bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo to primary labyrinthitis and discharge the patient without lumbar puncture when fever and headache are co-present.
Do NOT delay empiric antibiotics awaiting culture speciation or MALDI-TOF results — empiric coverage must begin within 60 minutes of suspicion.
Do NOT omit adjunctive dexamethasone — it is recommended before or with the first antibiotic dose and may reduce the severity of cochlear inflammation.

Do NOT interpret negative blood cultures as evidence against bacterial meningitis — bacteremia in S. suis meningitis is frequently transient and blood cultures are often negative despite positive CSF culture.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for bacterial meningitis.
key_reasoning_points: Streptococcus suis is an occupational zoonotic bacterium acquired from pigs and raw pork; pig farmers, abattoir workers, and raw-pork handlers in Southeast and East Asia are the principal risk group — the occupational swine-contact history is the key epidemiological clue.

Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction (vertigo, broad-based gait, positive Romberg) are the hallmark complications of S. suis meningitis, occurring in approximately 50-66% of cases, and may appear early and dominate the presentation before classic meningeal signs are fully established.

The characteristic diagnostic pitfall in S. suis meningitis is misattribution of the bilateral hearing loss and dizziness to acute labyrinthitis (as occurred at the district clinic in this case) — the combination of occupational swine exposure, fever, and headache should mandate CSF analysis regardless of any prior ENT attribution.

CSF Gram stain showing Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains is consistent with streptococcal species; standard multiplex PCR panels do not include S. suis, and MALDI-TOF is required for definitive speciation.

Adjunctive dexamethasone given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose is recommended per IDSA 2004 and De Gans 2002 for all adults with suspected bacterial meningitis; cohort data suggest dexamethasone may reduce the severity of cochlear inflammation and hearing-loss sequelae in S. suis meningitis.
S. suis is typically penicillin- and ceftriaxone-susceptible; once susceptibilities are confirmed, de-escalation to penicillin G or ceftriaxone monotherapy is appropriate.

red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo presenting before meningismus is fully established, initially diagnosed as acute labyrinthitis at the district clinic
red_herrings.intended_effect: A naive agent may accept the prior labyrinthitis diagnosis and focus workup on ENT causes, deferring lumbar puncture and missing the underlying bacterial meningitis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: In a febrile pig farmer, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction is the hallmark early presentation of S. suis meningitis; fever and headache mandate CSF analysis and the prior ENT attribution must be reconsidered.

red_herrings.data_point: Negative blood cultures (all bottles, no growth at 5 days)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Negative blood cultures may falsely reassure the clinician or agent that there is no systemic bacterial infection, potentially leading to premature de-escalation or abandonment of the bacterial meningitis diagnosis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Bacteremia in S. suis meningitis is frequently transient; negative blood cultures do not exclude the diagnosis and the confirmatory test is CSF culture, not blood culture.

metadata.real_seed_note: Seeded from: Petcharat C et al. 'Meningitis Caused by Streptococcus suis: Case Report and Review of the Literature.' PMC3325437, PMID 22523518, CC-BY-NC 3.0. The seed describes a 57-year-old male former pig farmer presenting with fever, headache, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with S. suis isolated from CSF; blood cultures were negative. The present case is a distinct fictional patient (56-year-old active pig farmer, Vietnam, different lab trajectory) inspired by this verified case. PMID verified on PubMed 2026-06-17.
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction present before full meningismus, creating a plausible primary ENT misdiagnosis (labyrinthitis) that an attentive agent must reject based on fever, occupational swine exposure, and progressive headache. Requires synthesis of occupational history, CSF findings (Gram-positive cocci requiring MALDI-TOF speciation, not in standard PCR panels), and understanding of the S. suis-specific hearing-loss complication and dexamethasone rationale.

vocab_gap: Formal pure-tone audiometry for objective SNHL quantification is a clinically relevant follow-up investigation for S. suis meningitis but is not in the closed order_specialized_test vocabulary (nearest in-vocabulary proxy is 'baep', a different test). Hearing loss is described clinically in the neurological exam and HPI. Recommend adding 'pure_tone_audiometry' to the vocabulary in a future update.
